definition: Intransigent means refusing to compromise or change a position.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word intransigent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know intransigent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Both other landlords trimmed their asking prices; the third stayed intransigent, and his corner lot sat empty for years.
Firm holds a position but can still hear reasons — it stops well short of intransigent.
Stubborn digs in past most persuasion, yet stops short of intransigent, which refuses the very idea of compromise.

Unyielding means refusing to give ground under pressure -- the position simply does not move, however hard it is pushed. It can describe a wall or a will as easily as a person. Intransigent is narrower and always about negotiation: not just holding ground, but rejecting the very process of compromise.

Uncompromising means holding out for all of it, every time -- and it is often praise: an uncompromising editor upholds a standard whole. Intransigent never compliments; it is the negotiator's accusation, aimed at the party that refuses to deal at all.

The novelist proved intransigent, and the book finally shipped with every last semicolon intact.
Intransigent is stronger than stubborn: the stubborn dig in against persuasion, while the intransigent reject the very idea of negotiating.
In- ('not') + transigere ('to drive a deal through') — someone who will not transact.
Intransigent is the negotiator's word — for the party that rejects compromise itself, not just your latest offer.
Stubborn is character; intransigent is posture at the table, and it shades critical: calling someone intransigent all but accuses them of bad faith.

The musicians' guild and the concert hall had settled every contract since 1974 in a single friendly afternoon.
This year the hall's new owner sent word that the old pay scale was 'not a starting point but a relic,' and then declined to say what the starting point was.
The guild offered three proposals in a week.

Asked to name any figure at all, the owner's lawyer repeated that the matter was 'not currently negotiable.' The arbitrator's notes, later made public, used one word for the owner's posture: intransigent -- not hard bargaining, but a refusal to bargain.
The autumn season opened with a string quartet of retired teachers playing to a half-empty hall, and the guild picketing politely outside.
